Complete and Reversible Reactions
Complete and Reversible ReactionsSection 3.1
✔
Objectives of this chapter
  • Distinguish a complete (irreversible) reaction from a reversible (limited) one.
  • Describe the dynamic equilibrium: equal rates, constant concentrations, reached from both sides.
  • Write the equilibrium law and calculate the equilibrium constant Kc.
  • Compare the reaction quotient Q with K to find the direction of evolution.
  • Use the degree of conversion α and the yield; study the esterification equilibrium.
  • Read data (K or α versus temperature) to find if a reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
  • Find the composition of the equilibrium state and the degree of dissociation.
  • Apply Le Chatelier’s principle (liquid phase): effect of a change in concentration and in temperature.

3.1.1 Action verbs in exam questions

Official exam questions use precise action verbs. Each verb asks for a specific kind of answer: learn them well.

Action verbWhat is expected
Define / Stategive the definition, the law or the rule, without justification
Name / Give / Writename a species, give a value or an expression, write an equation or a formula
Calculate / Determineuse a formula or a table and show the numerical result with its unit
Draw / Plot / Representconstruct a table, a diagram or a graph
Completefill in the missing data of a table or an equation
Identify / Specify / Indicatepick out the species, the direction or the observation asked for
Comparestate the similarities and the differences, or which one is larger
Deducedraw a conclusion from the data or from a previous result
Justify / Explaingive the reason, using a law, a calculation or a comparison (for example Q with Kc)
Show that / Verifycarry out the calculation and check the given result
Interpret / Describeread a graph or a table and say what it shows
 ◆ Complete (irreversible) reaction
A reaction is complete when it takes place in one direction only, from the reactants to the products, until at least one reactant is totally consumed (the limiting reactant). It is written with one arrow →. Example: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O.
 ◆ Reversible (incomplete) reaction
A reaction is reversible when the reactants form the products (forward reaction) and, at the same time, the products react to re-form the reactants (backward reaction). It is limited: no reactant is totally consumed, even if the reaction lasts a long time. It is written with two arrows ⇌. Examples: a) 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 and b) N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3
c) H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI and d) CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O
★
Closed system and homogeneous system
  • A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium only in a closed system: nothing enters or leaves, so the products can meet again and react.
  • A system is homogeneous when it contains one single phase: a mixture of gases, or a liquid (aqueous) solution. The equilibria of this chapter are homogeneous. (A mixture of solids and gas, or of immiscible liquids, is not homogeneous.)
✔
Correction to remember
▶

A homogeneous system is not defined as “all liquids or all gases but not solids”. The criterion is one single phase. A solution of a solid dissolved in water is also homogeneous.

3.1.3 Exercise: Practice: complete or reversible?

3.1.4 Exercise: Level 1 – Classify the reactions

Say whether each reaction is complete or reversible and justify with the arrow used.

a) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2

b) 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3

c) AgNO3 + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO3

d) H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI

e) CH3COOH + CH3OH ⇌ CH3COOCH3 + H2O.

f) Identify the systems that must be closed to reach equilibrium.

✔
Solution a)
▶

Complete (one arrow).

b) Reversible (⇌).

c) Complete (one arrow).

d) Reversible.

e) Reversible (esterification).

f) b, d and e: the reversible reactions need a closed system.

3.1.5 Exercise: Level 2 – What is present?

  1. 00 mol of SO2 and 0.50 mol of O2 are placed in a closed vessel with a catalyst. After a long time the mixture is analyzed.

a) Write the equation of the reaction.

b) Name the substances present in the final mixture.

c) Deduce whether the amount of SO2 can become zero. Explain.

d) Calculate the maximum amount of SO3 that could be formed and specify whether it is reached.

✔
Solution a)
▶

2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3.

b) SO2, O2 and SO3: the three substances are present.

c) No: the reaction is reversible and limited; the backward reaction re-forms SO2.

d) If the reaction were complete: n(SO3)max = 1.00 mol (both reactants are in stoichiometric proportion). In a reversible reaction this value is not reached: n(SO3) < 1.00 mol.

The Chemical Equilibrium
The Chemical EquilibriumSection 3.2
⇌

Live Simulation · Dynamic Equilibrium — H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2 HI

animated
Watch r₁ fall and r₂ rise until they meet — concentrations then stay constant (dynamic equilibrium).
The forward rate decreases as reactants are consumed; the backward rate increases as product accumulates. When r₁ = r₂ ≠ 0, the composition is constant: this is a dynamic equilibrium (the reactions continue, molecule by molecule).

★
What the graphs show
  • The amount of each reactant decreases (8 → 4 mol) and the amount of the product increases (0 → 8 mol).
  • From t = 32 min the amounts no longer change: 4 mol of H2, 4 mol of I2, 8 mol of HI. The system is in chemical equilibrium.
  • The reactants are not consumed: 4 mol of each remain; the reaction is limited.

3.2.2 Rates of the two reactions

◆
Dynamic chemical equilibrium

A reversible reaction reaches a state of dynamic chemical equilibrium when the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the backward reaction:

At equilibrium the concentrations (and amounts) of all species are constant. At the microscopic level the two reactions continue at the same rate: each second as many HI molecules are formed as are decomposed. The equilibrium is dynamic.

✎
Dynamic, not static

Nothing seems to change at equilibrium, yet the species keep reacting in both directions at the same rate. Think of a shop where people enter and leave at the same rate: the crowd keeps the same size, but the people are different.

✔
Correction to remember
▶

At equilibrium the reaction does not stop: it appears to stop at the macroscopic level only because the amounts are constant. The old expression “stationary (stop) phase” is wrong; say “dynamic equilibrium”.

★
Characteristics of the equilibrium
  • It is reached in a closed system at constant temperature, from a reversible reaction.
  • The composition is constant: [A], [B], [C], [D] do not change with time.
  • It is dynamic: r1 = r2 ≠ 0.
  • It can be reached from the reactants or from the products (the same state for the same total composition).
  • A catalyst makes the equilibrium reached faster but does not change the composition at equilibrium (see the Chapter of chemical kinetics).

3.2.3 Equilibrium reached from both sides

At a certain temperature the reaction H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI has an equilibrium constant Kc = 4 (it is defined in section 3.3). Two experiments are done in a 1.00 L vessel: (1) 1.00 mol of H2 and 1.00 mol of I2; (2) 2.00 mol of HI only.

★
Conclusion

In both cases the mixture ends with [H2] = [I2] = 0.50 mol/L and [HI] = 1.00 mol/L. The two mixtures contain the same total amount of each element (2 mol of H, 2 mol of I), so they reach the same equilibrium state.

✔

3.2.4 Exercise: Practice: the dynamic equilibrium

3.2.5 Exercise: Level 1 – True or false?

Correct the false statements.

a) At equilibrium all reactions stop.

b) At equilibrium the concentrations of the reactants and of the products are equal.

c) At equilibrium r1 = r2.

d) A reversible reaction can reach equilibrium in an open vessel.

e) A catalyst increases the amount of products at equilibrium.

f) The same equilibrium can be reached starting from the products.

✔
Solution a)
▶

False: both reactions continue (dynamic equilibrium).

b) False: the concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.

c) True.

d) False: a closed system is needed.

e) False: it only reduces the time needed to reach equilibrium.

f) True (for the same overall composition).

3.2.6 Exercise: Level 2 – Analyzing a table

The reaction N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2 is studied in a closed 1.0 L vessel. Starting with 0.200 mol of N2O4, the amounts are measured.

t (s): 0, 20, 40, 60, 80.

n(N2O4) (mol): 0.200, 0.120, 0.104, 0.101, 0.100.

a) Calculate n(NO2) at each time.

b) From what time is the equilibrium reached? Justify.

c) Draw the graph of n(N2O4) and of n(NO2) versus time (separately).

d) Calculate the average rate of disappearance of N2O4 between 0 and 20 s, then between 40 and 60 s. Compare and explain.

✔
Solution a)
▶

n(NO2) = 2 × (0.200 − n(N2O4)): 0, 0.160, 0.192, 0.198, 0.200 mol.

b) From t = 80 s: the amounts no longer change (0.100 mol and 0.200 mol) (the change before is less than 0.001 mol).

c) N2O4 decreases from 0.200 to 0.100 mol; NO2 increases from 0 to 0.200 mol (see the figure, in mol/L the shape is the same).

d) 0–20 s: (0.200 − 0.120)/20 = 4.0×10−3 mol/s; 40–60 s: (0.104 − 0.101)/20 = 1.5×10−4 mol/s. The rate decreases because the concentration of the reactant decreases and the backward reaction becomes faster; at equilibrium it is zero (net).

3.2.7 Exercise: Level 2 – Both sides

At 450 °C the equilibrium H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI has Kc = 50. The experiment is done in a 1.00 L vessel:

  1. 50 mol H2 + 0.50 mol I2 + 1.00 mol HI.

Calculate Q at t = 0 for experiment C and find the direction in which it evolves.

✔
Solution
▶

In Experiment C: Q = [HI]2/([H2][I2]) = 1.002/(0.50 × 0.50) = 4.0 < Kc: experiment C is not at equilibrium and the reaction must evolve in the forward direction.

The Equilibrium Law and the Constant K
The Equilibrium Law and the Constant KSection 3.3
◆
Equilibrium constant Kc

For a reversible reaction in a homogeneous system at equilibrium,

aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the ratio below is a constant at a given temperature. It is called the equilibrium constant Kc (the law of mass action, or equilibrium law):

The concentrations are the equilibrium concentrations, in mol/L. The products are on top, the reactants at the bottom, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.

★
Rules for writing Kc
  • Kc has no unit (it is written as a pure number).
  • Gases and dissolved species are written; a pure solid or a pure liquid is not written.
  • In a dilute aqueous solution, the solvent water is not written.
  • In a homogeneous liquid mixture where water is a reactant or a product (as in the esterification), H2O is written, because it is one of the species in the same phase.
  • The expression depends on how the equation is written (the coefficients).
EquilibriumExpression of Kc
N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3Kc = [NH3]2 / ([N2][H2]3)
2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3Kc = [SO3]2 / ([SO2]2[O2])
H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HIKc = [HI]2 / ([H2][I2])
N2O4 ⇌ 2NO2Kc = [NO2]2 / [N2O4]
CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2OKc = [CH3COOC2H5][H2O] / ([CH3COOH][C2H5OH])
Fe3+ + SCN− ⇌ FeSCN2+ (dilute aqueous)Kc = [FeSCN2+] / ([Fe3+][SCN−]) (water not written)

Example 1 – Calculating Kc. In the reaction H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI of section 3.2 the equilibrium amounts in a vessel of volume V are 4, 4 and 8 mol:

✎
Volume cancels

When the number of moles of gas is the same on both sides (here 2 = 1 + 1), the volume cancels and Kc can be calculated with the amounts (mol). This is not true in general (for N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 you must use concentrations).

3.3.1 Example: H2O + CO ⇌ H2 + CO2 (three mixtures)

The reaction H2O + CO ⇌ H2 + CO2 is studied at one temperature. Three mixtures are prepared; the concentrations (mol/L) before the reaction and at equilibrium are measured.

 Mixture 1Mixture 2Mixture 3
Before: [CO] ; [H2O]0.0243 ; 0.02430 ; 00.0300 ; 0.0100
Before: [CO2] ; [H2]0 ; 00.0468 ; 0.04680.0400 ; 0.0300
Equilibrium: [CO] ; [H2O]0.0135 ; 0.01350.0260 ; 0.02600.0410 ; 0.0210
Equilibrium: [CO2] ; [H2]0.0108 ; 0.01080.0208 ; 0.02080.0290 ; 0.0190
Kc = [CO2][H2] / ([CO][H2O])0.6400.6400.640
★
Conclusion

The equilibrium concentrations are different in the three mixtures, but the ratio Kc is always 0.640. Kc depends only on the temperature (and on the equation), not on the initial amounts. Mixture 1 starts from the reactants only, mixture 2 from the products only, mixture 3 from both: the equilibrium is reached from both sides.

✔

3.3.2 Exercise: Practice: the equilibrium constant

3.3.3 Exercise: Level 1 – Write Kc

Write the expression of Kc.

a) 2NO + O2 ⇌ 2NO2 b) PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2

c) CO + 2H2 ⇌ CH3OH (all gases) d) 2NH3 ⇌ N2 + 3H2

e) CH3COOH + CH3OH ⇌ CH3COOCH3 + H2O (liquid mixture)

f) Ag+ + Cl− ⇌ AgCl (dilute aqueous solution: only the dissolved species)

✔
Solution f)
▶

For the dissolved ions only: Kc = 1/([Ag+][Cl−]) if AgCl is a solid (it is not written).

3.3.4 Exercise: Level 2 – Kc from equilibrium amounts

In a 2.0 L vessel, 1.0 mol of N2 and 3.0 mol of H2 give at equilibrium 0.40 mol of NH3: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3. a) Draw the progress table (amounts) and determine x at equilibrium. b) Calculate the equilibrium concentrations. c) Calculate Kc. d) Justify why the volume can not be ignored here.

✔
Solution
▶

n(NH3) = 2x = 0.40 ⇒ x = 0.20 mol; n(N2) = 0.80 mol, n(H2) = 2.40 mol.

b) [N2] = 0.80/2.0 = 0.40; [H2] = 2.40/2.0 = 1.20; [NH3] = 0.40/2.0 = 0.20 mol/L.

d) The number of moles of gas changes (4 → 2): the volume does not cancel, so the concentrations (not the amounts) must be used.

3.3.5 Exercise: Level 3 – Equation written two ways

At a given temperature Kc = 4.0 for H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI (reaction 1).

a) Find Kc for 2HI ⇌ H2 + I2 (reaction 2).

b) Find Kc for 2H2 + 2I2 ⇌ 4HI (reaction 3).

c) Find Kc for 1/2 H2 + 1/2 I2 ⇌ HI (reaction 4).

d) Conclude: how does Kc change when the equation is reversed, multiplied by n?

Kc = 4 is an arbitrary hypothetical value not a real value

✔
Solution d)
▶

Reversed equation: K becomes 1/K. Equation multiplied by n: K becomes K(n).

The Reaction Quotient Q: Direction of Evolution
The Reaction Quotient Q: Direction of EvolutionSection 3.4
Q

Interactive · Reaction Quotient Q vs Kc — Direction of Evolution

drag the slider
═ EQUILIBRIUM ═
Q = 0.00
Q value
Kc = 4
◆
Reaction quotient Q

At any instant (not only at equilibrium) the reaction quotient Q has the same expression as Kc but uses the instantaneous concentrations:

At equilibrium, Q = Kc.

★
Criterion of evolution
  • Q < Kc: the mixture has too many reactants; it evolves in the forward direction: reactants are consumed, products formed; Q increases up to Kc.
  • Q = Kc: the system is at equilibrium; the composition does not change.
  • Q > Kc: the mixture has too many products; it evolves in the backward direction: products are consumed; Q decreases down to Kc.
  • Q = 0 (no products at the start) ⇒ the system evolves in the forward direction. • Q → ∞ (no reactants at the start) ⇒ backward direction.

Example 2 – In the previous experiment. In H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI (Kc = 4) at t = 16 min the amounts were 6, 6 and 4 mol:

Example 3 – Methane and hydrogen sulfide. The reaction CH4 + 2H2S ⇌ CS2 + 4H2 has Kc = 3.59 at 900 °C (all gases). Three mixtures (mol/L) are prepared:

Mixture[CH4][H2S][CS2][H2]QDirection
11.001.001.001.001.00Q < Kc: forward direction
20.200.200.302.00600Q > Kc: backward direction
31.001.003.591.003.59Q = Kc: equilibrium
★
Kc depends on the temperature only

Kc does not depend on the initial concentrations, on the catalyst, or on the volume; it depends only on the temperature (and on the way the equation is written). When a concentration is changed by adding or removing a species at constant temperature, Kc is the same: calculate the new Q and compare it with Kc to know how the system evolves, then calculate the new equilibrium.

✔
Correction to remember
▶

Write Kc with no unit. The value of Kc given at a temperature belongs to the equation written; a catalyst or a change of the initial amounts never changes it.

✔

3.4.1 Exercise: Practice: the reaction quotient

3.4.2 Exercise: Level 1 – Direction of evolution

At a given temperature Kc = 50 for H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI (volume V = 1.0 L).

For each mixture calculate Q and give the direction of evolution.

a) 1.0 mol H2, 1.0 mol I2, 0 mol HI.

b) 0.10 mol H2, 0.10 mol I2, 2.0 mol HI.

c) 0.20 mol H2, 0.20 mol I2, 1.4 mol HI.

d) 0.40 mol H2, 0.50 mol I2, 2.0 mol HI.

✔
Solution a)
▶

Q = 0 < 50 ⇒ forward direction.

b) Q = 2.02/(0.10 × 0.10) = 400 > 50 ⇒ backward direction.

c) Q = 1.42/(0.20 × 0.20) = 49 ≈ 50 (< 50) ⇒ forward direction, very close to equilibrium.

d) Q = 2.02/(0.40 × 0.50) = 20 < 50 ⇒ forward direction.

3.4.3 Exercise: Level 2 – Adding a reactant

At equilibrium in a 1.00 L vessel, H2 + I2 ⇌ 2HI contains 0.50 mol of H2, 0.50 mol of I2 and 1.00 mol of HI (Kc = 4). 0.50 mol of H2 is then added at constant temperature and volume.

a) Calculate Q just after the addition. In which direction does the system evolve?

b) Draw the progress table of the new evolution and determine x.

c) Give the new composition.

✔
Solution a)
▶

[H2] = 1.00 mol/L; Q = 1.002/(1.00 × 0.50) = 2.0 < 4 ⇒ forward direction (formation of HI).

c) n(H2) = 0.900 mol, n(I2) = 0.400 mol, n(HI) = 1.200 mol. Check: Q = 1.2002/(0.900 × 0.400) = 4.0 = Kc ✔.

Composition of the Equilibrium State, Degree of Conversion and Degree of Dissociation
Composition of the Equilibrium State, Degree of Conversion and Degree of DissociationSection 3.5
α

Interactive · Degree of Dissociation α — Particle Picture

drag to dissociate

3.5.1 Composition of the equilibrium state

◆
Composition

The composition of the equilibrium state is given by the amounts (numbers of moles) n of all the species present at equilibrium, or by their concentrations C = n/V (mol/L). These values are constant in time; they depend on the initial amounts, on the temperature and on Kc.

★
How to find the composition
  1. Write the equation and the expression of Kc. 2. Build the progress table in moles: ni(eq) = ni(initial) ∓ (coefficient) × xeq, with the same x for all the species. 3. Determine xeq: either it is deduced from a measurement (the amount or the concentration of one species at equilibrium), or it is calculated from Kc written with the equilibrium concentrations. 4. Calculate the amounts and the concentrations (divide by V). 5. Check: Q = Kc with the equilibrium values.

Example 4 – Composition from Kc. In a solution, A + B ⇌ C + D has Kc = 9.0. The initial concentrations are [A]0 = [B]0 = 1.0 mol/L and no C or D. With x the concentration of A that has reacted:

Composition: [A] = [B] = 0.25 mol/L; [C] = [D] = 0.75 mol/L. In 0.50 L of solution the amounts are 0.125 mol of A and of B, and 0.375 mol of C and of D. (Check: 0.752/0.252 = 9.0 ✔.)

Example – When the volume matters. In the solution equilibrium Fe3+ + SCN− ⇌ FeSCN2+ there are two species on the left and one on the right: the volume does not cancel and the moles must be converted into concentrations. A mixture of volume 0.500 L at equilibrium contains 0.0040 mol of Fe3+, 0.0020 mol of SCN− and 0.0060 mol of FeSCN2+.

[Fe3+] = 0.0040/0.500 = 0.0080; [SCN−] = 0.0020/0.500 = 0.0040; [FeSCN2+] = 0.0060/0.500 = 0.012 mol/L.

✔
Correction to remember
▶

Using the moles directly would give 0.0060/(0.0040 × 0.0020) = 750, which is wrong. The volume cancels in Kc only when the number of moles is the same on both sides of the equation.

3.5.2 What does the value of Kc tell us?

Value of KcComposition at equilibriumConclusion
Kc < 10−3mostly reactantsthe reaction hardly takes place
10−3 < Kc < 103significant amounts of reactants and productsa real equilibrium
Kc > 103mostly productsthe reaction is nearly complete
 ✔ Careful
Kc tells how far the reaction goes, not how fast. A reaction with a very large Kc can still be very slow (Chapters 1 and 2).		 

3.5.3 Degree of conversion

◆
Degree of conversion α of a reactant

The degree of conversion (or advancement) of a reactant is the fraction of its initial amount that has reacted at equilibrium:

It is calculated for the limiting reactant (or for any reactant when the mixture is stoichiometric). 0 ≤ α ≤ 1; it is often given as a percentage.

★
Complete or reversible?
  • Complete reaction: xeq = xmax, so α = 1 (100 %) for the limiting reactant (the other reactant may remain in excess). Do not say α = 1 for “each” reactant: only the limiting one (or both if they were in exact stoichiometric proportion) is totally consumed.
  • Reversible reaction: xeq < xmax, so α < 1.
  • The yield of a product is n(product) obtained ÷ n(product) expected if the reaction were complete: for a limiting reactant it is equal to α.

3.5.4 Degree of dissociation

◆
Degree of dissociation α

When the reactant is a species that splits into two (or more) species, AB ⇌ A + B, its degree of conversion is called its degree of dissociation α: the fraction of the initial amount of AB that has dissociated,

If n0 mol of AB are introduced, the table in α gives the whole composition (amounts) without any other unknown. With C0 = n0/V the constant becomes Kc = C0 α2 / (1 − α). α depends on the temperature and on the concentration (a more dilute solution is more dissociated).

Example 5 – Table in α. n mol of PCl5 are heated in a closed vessel: PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2. Let α be the degree of dissociation of PCl5:

 PCl5PCl3Cl2Total (mol)
Initialn00n
Equilibriumn(1 − α)nαnαn(1 + α)
✎
Conversion or dissociation?

The two words describe the same quantity (the fraction of the reactant that has reacted at equilibrium). “Dissociation” is used when the reactant splits into simpler species (PCl5, N2O4, an acid in water); “conversion” is used for any reactant of any reaction.

The Esterification Equilibrium
The Esterification EquilibriumSection 3.6
⇌

Interactive · Esterification Yield — Effect of Alcohol Excess

change the alcohol

Fixed: 1.00 mol ethanoic acid, Kc = 4. Slide the alcohol amount to see how Le Chatelier's idea (excess of a reactant) raises the yield from 67 % toward 100 %.

1.00 mol
Yield
◆
Esterification and hydrolysis

A carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol and forms an ester and water. The reaction is slow, limited and athermic (very small heat); it is the only organic equilibrium of the course. The backward reaction is the hydrolysis of the ester:

CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O

ethanoic acid + ethanol ⇌ ethyl ethanoate + water. The catalyst is a few drops of concentrated H2SO4 (heating also speeds it up).

✔
Correction to remember
▶

The ester formed is ethyl ethanoate, CH3COOC2H5 (not “CH2COOC2H5”) and the alcohol is ethanol, C2H5OH (not “CH2CH2OH”).

CompoundCondensed formulaName
Carboxylic acidR–COOH, e.g. CH3COOHethanoic acid
AlcoholR'–OH, e.g. C2H5OHethanol
EsterR–COO–R', e.g. CH3COOC2H5ethyl ethanoate
WaterH2Owater
★
Equilibrium constant

All four species are in one liquid phase, so the water is written:

The volume cancels (2 = 2). For a primary alcohol and an equimolar mixture, Kc ≈ 4 at any temperature (the reaction is athermic, so Kc does not depend on T).

Example 6 – Equimolar mixture. 1.00 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.00 mol of ethanol react (Kc = 4):

Stagex (mol)CH3COOHC2H5OHesterH2O
Initial01.0001.0000.0000.000
At advancement xx1.000 − x1.000 − xxx
Equilibrium0.6670.3330.3330.6670.667

The yield is α = x/1.00 = 67 %. The mixture contains 0.333 mol of acid, 0.333 mol of alcohol, 0.667 mol of ester and 0.667 mol of water.

3.6.1 How to increase the yield?

These two changes are applications of Le Chatelier’s principle (section 3.8).

★
Two ways, explained with Q
  • Use an excess of one reactant (usually the cheaper alcohol): with 1 mol of acid and 3 mol of alcohol:

3x2 − 16x + 12 = 0 ⇒ x = 0.903 mol, yield 90 % (instead of 67 %).

  • Remove one product (distill the ester, remove water): Q becomes smaller than Kc, so the system evolves in the forward direction and more ester is formed.
✎
Class of the alcohol

With an equimolar mixture the yield is about 67 % for a primary alcohol, about 60 % for a secondary alcohol and about 5 % for a tertiary alcohol. A catalyst or heating makes the equilibrium faster but does not change the yield.

✎
Hydrolysis

The backward reaction (ester + water ⇌ acid + alcohol) is also limited. Starting with 1 mol of ester and 1 mol of water, K = 1/4 gives y/(1 − y) = 1/2, so only 33 % of the ester is hydrolyzed.

✔

Kc = 4 for the esterification of ethanoic acid by ethanol.

a) 1.00 mol of acid and 2.00 mol of ethanol are mixed: find the yield.

New equilibrium (y mol more ester): 4 = (0.667 + y)(0.267 + y)/(0.333 − y)2 ⇒ 3y2 − 3.6y + 0.267 = 0 ⇒ y = 0.079 mol. n(ester) = 0.746 mol: yield 75 % (instead of 67 %).

Temperature and the Equilibrium Constant
Temperature and the Equilibrium ConstantSection 3.7
🌡

Interactive · Temperature & Color — N₂O₄ ⇌ 2 NO₂

heat / cool
Gas mixture
color ↔ brown
25 °C
★
Kc versus temperature

Kc changes only with the temperature. The experiments show:

  • Endothermic forward reaction (ΔH > 0): Kc increases when T increases; the equilibrium amount of products increases with T.
  • Exothermic forward reaction (ΔH < 0): Kc decreases when T increases; the amount of products decreases with T.
  • Athermic reaction (ΔH ≈ 0), such as the esterification: Kc is constant.
✔
Writing ΔH

Write ΔH separately, with its sign: for example N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, ΔH < 0; do not write “+ΔH” among the products.

3.7.1 Reading data to find the sign of ΔH

★
Method
  1. Find how Kc (or α, or the amount of product) varies when T increases.
  2. If it increases, the forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH > 0); if it decreases, the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH < 0).

The shift caused by a change of temperature is studied with Le Chatelier’s principle in section 3.8.

✎
Heating a system at equilibrium: use Q

At a temperature T1 the system is at equilibrium: Q = K1. If the temperature is raised to T2 (endothermic forward reaction) the constant becomes K2 > K1. Just after heating Q = K1 < K2, so the system evolves in the forward direction (1) until Q = K2.

✔

Shifting Equilibrium: Le Chatelier’s Principle
Shifting Equilibrium: Le Chatelier’s PrincipleSection 3.8
⚖

Interactive · Le Chatelier's Seesaw — A + B ⇌ C + D

add / remove
Reactants
A + B
50
Products
C + D
50
Reactants: Products:
★
Scope of this section

Le Chatelier’s principle is applied here only to homogeneous equilibria in the liquid phase (aqueous solutions and liquid mixtures such as the esterification). Two modifications are studied: a change in concentration and a change in temperature. (The effects of pressure and of volume on gas equilibria are not studied.)

3.8.1 What is a shift of the equilibrium?

◆
Shift of an equilibrium

A system at equilibrium is disturbed (modified from outside) when a species is added or removed, or when the temperature is changed. The system leaves its equilibrium state and evolves in the forward direction (toward the products, “to the right”) or in the backward direction (toward the reactants, “to the left”) until a new equilibrium state is reached, with a new composition: the equilibrium is shifted.

◆
Le Chatelier’s principle

When a modification is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the system evolves in the direction that tends to cancel (oppose) the effect of this modification, until a new equilibrium is reached.

✔
Correction to remember
▶

The principle is qualitative: it gives the direction of the evolution, not the amounts. The effect is only partly cancelled: if ethanol is added to an esterification mixture, part of it is consumed, but not all of the addition: its amount at the new equilibrium is larger than before the addition. To find the new composition, use Q, Kc and the progress table.

3.8.2 The effect of a change in concentration

★
Rules (constant temperature)
  • Adding a reactant, or removing a product: the system evolves in the forward direction (the added reactant is partly consumed; the removed product is partly re-formed).
  • Adding a product, or removing a reactant: the system evolves in the backward direction.
  • Why? Q changes at once while Kc does not change (same temperature): adding a reactant or removing a product makes Q < Kc (forward direction); the opposite change makes Q > Kc (backward direction). The system then evolves until Q = Kc again.

Example 7 – Esterification (liquid mixture). At equilibrium 0.60 mol of ethanoic acid and 0.60 mol of ethanol have given 0.40 mol of ester and 0.40 mol of water (Kc = 4.0, with 0.20 mol of each reactant left). 0.40 mol of ethanol is added.

The new equilibrium (y mol of additional ester): 4.0 = (0.40 + y)2/((0.20 − y)(0.60 − y)) gives y = 0.085 mol. New composition: acid 0.115 mol, ethanol 0.515 mol, ester 0.485 mol, water 0.485 mol. The ethanol (0.60 mol just after the addition) is only partly consumed, the acid is more converted, and the yield based on the acid rises from 67 % to 81 %.

Example 8 – Chromate and dichromate. In aqueous solution 2CrO42− + 2H3O+ ⇌ Cr2O72− + 3H2O: the yellow chromate ion is in equilibrium with the orange dichromate ion; Kc = [Cr2O72−]/([CrO42−]2[H3O+]2) (the solvent water is not written). Adding an acid increases [H3O+]: Q < Kc, forward direction: the solution turns orange. Adding a base consumes H3O⁺ (H3O+ + HO− → 2H2O), so [H3O+] decreases: Q > Kc, backward direction: the solution turns back yellow.

Example 10 – Iron (III) and thiocyanate. Fe3+ (pale yellow) + SCN− (colorless) ⇌ FeSCN2+ (blood red). Effect of each modification at constant temperature:

ModificationEffect on QShiftColor
Add Fe3+[Fe3+] increases: Q < Kcforward directiondarker red
Add SCN−[SCN−] increases: Q < Kcforward directiondarker red
Add oxalate ions (they remove Fe3+)[Fe3+] decreases: Q > Kcbackward directionlighter, paler
Add water (dilution)all concentrations decrease; Q > Kc (one species in the numerator, two in the denominator)backward directionlighter (dilution and shift)
✎ Catalyst and solvent
• A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium: it speeds up both reactions equally (Chapter of kinetic factors).
• In the esterification the water is a species of the mixture (it is written in Kc): adding water favors the hydrolysis (backward direction). In a dilute aqueous solution the solvent water is not written in Kc.		 ✎ Catalyst and solvent
• A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium: it speeds up both reactions equally (Chapter of kinetic factors).
• In the esterification the water is a species of the mixture (it is written in Kc): adding water favors the hydrolysis (backward direction). In a dilute aqueous solution the solvent water is not written in Kc.		 ✎ Catalyst and solvent
• A catalyst does not shift the equilibrium: it speeds up both reactions equally (Chapter of kinetic factors).
• In the esterification the water is a species of the mixture (it is written in Kc): adding water favors the hydrolysis (backward direction). In a dilute aqueous solution the solvent water is not written in Kc.

3.8.3 The effect of a change in temperature

★
Rules (a change of temperature changes Kc)
  • Heating (raising the temperature): the system evolves in the direction that absorbs heat, the endothermic direction.
  • Cooling (lowering the temperature): the system evolves in the direction that releases heat, the exothermic direction.
★
Why?

Temperature is the only quantity that changes Kc. For an endothermic forward reaction Kc increases when T increases (section 3.7): just after heating, Q (still equal to the old Kc) is smaller than the new Kc, so the system evolves in the forward direction; this agrees with the principle (the heat is absorbed). Conversely, a shift observed experimentally allows to deduce the sign of ΔH.

Example 9 – Cobalt (II) chloride. In solution [Co(H2O)6]2+ + 4Cl− ⇌ [CoCl4]2− + 6H2O the complex on the left is pink and that on the right is blue (Kc = [CoCl42−]/([Co(H2O)62+][Cl−]4); water is the solvent). The solution is violet at 25 °C, blue when heated and pink when cooled in ice. Heating shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction, so forward direction is endothermic (ΔH > 0); cooling shifts it in the backward direction (exothermic).

When the temperature is raised, the system does not respond instantly: the rates change and the composition drifts gradually to the new equilibrium (no sudden jump, unlike the addition of a species).

✎
Esterification: no shift with temperature

The esterification is athermic: Kc stays equal to about 4 at any temperature, so heating does not shift the equilibrium and does not change the yield; it only makes the equilibrium reached faster.

3.8.4 Summary of the shifts

ModificationShiftEffect on Kc
Add a reactantforward directionnone
Remove a reactantbackward directionnone
Add a productbackward directionnone
Remove a productforward directionnone
Heat an exothermic forward reactionbackward directionKc decreases
Heat an endothermic forward reactionforward directionKc increases
Cool an exothermic forward reactionforward directionKc increases
Cool an endothermic forward reactionbackward directionKc decreases
Add a catalystno shift (equilibrium reached faster)none
★
Big ideas
  • Equilibrium is dynamic: the rates of the forward and the backward reactions are equal and the concentrations are constant.
  • A change in concentration shifts the equilibrium but never changes Kc.
  • A change in temperature shifts the equilibrium and changes Kc.
  • A catalyst neither shifts the equilibrium nor changes Kc.
  • Le Chatelier: the system evolves so as to partly oppose the modification.
✔

3.8.10 Exercise: Level 3 – Reading a graph with two modifications

Use Figure 3.24, in which two modifications of the equilibrium A + B ⇌ C + D (liquid) are made at t1 = 20 min and t2 = 50 min. Before t1 the equilibrium concentrations are [A] = [B] = 0.40 and [C] = [D] = 0.60 mol/L. a) Identify the modification made at t1. Give the amount added per liter. b) Justify the increase of [C] and [D] after t1, using Q. c) After t2 the concentrations of C and D decrease to 0.60 mol/L while [A] = 0.40 and [B] = 0.80 mol/L. The temperature was raised at t2. Calculate Kc at the new temperature and compare with 2.25. d) Deduce whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic. Justify with Le Chatelier’s principle.

✔
Solution a)
▶

[B] jumps from 0.40 to 0.80 mol/L: 0.40 mol of B per liter was added.

b) Q = 0.602/(0.40 × 0.80) = 1.125 < Kc = 2.25 ⇒ forward direction: C and D are formed.

d) Heating shifted the equilibrium in the backward direction (Kc decreased): heating favors the endothermic direction, so the backward reaction is endothermic and the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH < 0).

3.9.6 Summary of the chapter

TopicKey points
Reactionscomplete (→, limiting reactant consumed, α = 1) and reversible (⇌, limited, 0< α < 1)
Equilibriumclosed system, dynamic: r1 = r2, constant concentrations, reached from both sides
LawKc = [C]c[D]d / ([A]a[B]b), no unit, solids and solvent not written, depends on T only
Q versus KcQ < K: forward direction; Q = K: equilibrium; Q > K: backward direction
Equation changesreversed: 1/K; multiplied by n: Kn
α and yieldα = xeq/xmax; table in x or in α
Esterificationslow, limited, athermic; K ≈ 4; 67 % (primary), 60 % (secondary), 5 % (tertiary)
Increase the yieldexcess of a reactant, removal of a product; a catalyst does not change K or the yield
Temperatureendothermic: K increases with T; exothermic: K decreases with T; athermic: K constant
Compositionprogress table in x (mol or mol/L); Kc = [C]c[D]d/([A]a[B]b) gives x
Degree of dissociationα = ndissociated/ninitial; Kc = C0α2/(1 − α) for A ⇌ B + C
Le Chatelier (liquid phase)add a reactant / remove a product: forward direction; add a product / remove a reactant: backward direction; heating: endothermic direction; catalyst: no shift

3.9.7 Exercise: Mixed practice

3.9.8 Exercise: Level 2 – Find the mistakes

Correct each statement. (1) “At equilibrium the reaction stops.” (2) “Kc increases when a catalyst is added.” (3) “In a complete reaction both reactants have α = 1.” (4) “Kc = 4 mol/L.” (5) “A homogeneous system contains only liquids.” (6) “If Q > Kc the reaction evolves in the forward direction.”

✔
Solution
▶

(1) It is dynamic: r1 = r2 ≠ 0.

(2) A catalyst does not change Kc; only the temperature does for the thermic reactions

(3) α = 1 only for the limiting reactant.

(4) Kc is written with no unit0.

(5) A homogeneous system has one single phase (gases or a solution).

(6) If Q > Kc the system evolves in the backward direction.

3.9.9 Exercise: Level 3 – Water−gas shift

For H2O + CO ⇌ H2 + CO2, Kc = 0.640 at a given temperature. A mixture of 0.10 mol of H2O and 0.10 mol of CO is placed in a 1.0 L vessel.

a) Draw the progress table and calculate x at equilibrium.

b) Give the equilibrium concentrations and α.

c) 0.10 mol of H2 is added at equilibrium. Calculate Q and find the direction.

✔
Solution b)
▶

[H2O] = [CO] = 0.0556 mol/L; [H2] = [CO2] = 0.0444 mol/L; α = 0.0444/0.10 = 0.44.

c) [H2] = 0.0444 + 0.10 = 0.1444: Q = (0.1444 × 0.0444)/(0.0556 × 0.0556) = 2.07 > 0.640 ⇒ backward direction.
